paragraphs: Plate-format PDMS microfluidic culture devices from hybrid SU-8/3D-printed resin wafer molds
Tristan Simas1,#, Yonatan Morocz2, Jathav Puvirajan1, David Juncker2, and Alyson Fournier1
1Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Montréal Neurological Institute, McGill University, Montréal, Québec, Canada
2Victor Phillip Dahdaleh Institute of Genomic Medicine, McGill University, Montréal, QC, Canada.
#Corresponding author
Abstract

Microfluidic platforms enable spatially controlled neuronal culture and compartment-specific manipulation, but their adoption in medium-throughput assays is limited by fabrication methods that require labor-intensive processing and assembly. Here, we present an open-source, hybrid microfabrication strategy for producing reusable silicon-wafer molds that integrate photolithographically defined microchannels with 3D-printed structures for simultaneous formation of culture wells. A parametric design framework, OpenMFD, generates coordinated photomasks and three-dimensional insert arrays, enabling precise alignment and simultaneous bonding of millimeter-scale structures to SU-8/SUEX-patterned wafers. Using this approach, we fabricated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) culture plates containing 48 compartmentalized devices arranged on a standard microplate grid, eliminating individual well punching during device production. Devices supported multichannel liquid handling, automated high-content imaging, directional fluidic manipulation, and primary cortical neuron culture. Compartmentalized axonal growth was demonstrated by retrograde cholera toxin B labeling establishing compatibility with parallel neuronal assays. Furthermore, the parametric design framework generated matched fabrication files for additional neuronal culture configurations, illustrating the adaptability of the approach. By combining high-resolution photolithography with scalable three-dimensional molding, this method provides an accessible and reusable fabrication platform for medium-throughput microfluidic assays.
Introduction

Microfluidic compartmentalization has transformed the study of neuronal cell biology by enabling independent access to cell bodies, axons and their local extracellular environments. Microchannel-connected culture chambers permit spatially restricted treatments, isolation of axonal material and analysis of axonal injury, regeneration and transport (PMID: 16094385). Subsequent designs have enabled controlled axon-guidance gradients, localized neuron–glia interactions and more complex neuronal networks (PMIDs: 26000554; 22828584; 35466333). The geometry of connecting microchannels also influences device performance and the study of communication between neuronal populations (PMID: 36111641). Together, these developments have established compartmentalized microfluidics as a versatile approach for investigating neuronal connectivity and responses to spatially defined perturbations.

Extending these experimental capabilities to parallel assays requires platforms that accommodate multiple treatment conditions, biological replicates and established liquid-handling and imaging workflows. A high-capacity microfluidic plate containing up to 96 independently addressable, three-compartment culture units has been used with primary rodent and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, demonstrating compatibility with morphological and functional measurements (PMID: 38150531). Other approaches prioritizing experimental flexibility include modular microfluidic units that can be combined into customizable neuronal culture configurations, whereas fluid-walled chambers support human neuronal microcircuits and moderate-throughput axotomy assays (PMIDs: 35466333; 38841815). These studies establish that parallelization and adaptable neuronal compartmentalization are feasible. Nevertheless, the fabrication workflow remains an important design consideration when laboratories need to reproduce, modify or manufacture custom arrays of devices.

A persistent fabrication challenge is the integration of micrometer-scale channels, which control neurite access and local fluid movement, with millimeter-scale reservoirs that permit straightforward cell seeding and pipetting. Conventional PDMS soft lithography can reproduce photolithographically defined microfeatures, but culture reservoirs are often opened individually after casting. This mismatch has previously been addressed with hybrid micro–macro molding combining milled and hot-embossed structures to replicate microscopic channels and macroscopic reservoirs without manual punching (PMID: 20049640). The approach was subsequently applied to multi-compartment neuron–glia cultures supporting localized treatments (PMID: 22828584). Other strategies use additive manufacturing to create compartmentalized neuronal devices without extensive manual post-processing (PMID: 32832365). Building on previous advances in multiscale molding and the elimination of manual reservoir punching, our approach introduces a customizable, parametric design strategy that enables the simultaneous alignment and assembly of large arrays of well-forming inserts onto reusable photolithographically patterned molds, facilitating reproducible, medium-throughput device fabrication.

Photopolymer-based 3D printing offers accessible fabrication of larger structures and complex geometries, although printed resins can inhibit PDMS curing and may require additional treatments before use as casting molds (PMID: 40190179). Hybrid assemblies combining soft lithography with printed polymer components provide another route to customizable biological microfluidic systems (PMID: 40667579). Parylene C coatings have also been shown to limit material degradation and cytotoxic leaching from printed resins in primary-cell applications (PMID: 37534979). Particularly relevant to neuronal compartmentalization, Ristola and colleagues combined SU-8 microfeatures with individually positioned 3D-printed metal inserts to fabricate neuron–oligodendrocyte culture devices (Ristola et al., 2019; DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ab16a7). This precedent demonstrates the feasibility of combining patterned wafers with tall inserts, while highlighting the importance of practical alignment and assembly procedures when extending such designs to larger arrays.

Here, we introduce OpenMFD, an open-source parametric design and hybrid fabrication workflow for producing reusable wafer-scale molds for medium-throughput microfluidic culture devices. Shared design coordinates generate matched photomasks, resin-insert arrays and plate components, enabling the simultaneous alignment and bonding of well-forming inserts to SU-8/SUEX-patterned silicon wafers. Photolithography defines the fine microchannels, while the retained printed inserts form the culture wells directly during each PDMS cast, removing the need for individual well punching in successive production runs. We demonstrate the approach using an array of 48 two-compartment neuronal devices containing 96 wells on a standard 9 mm plate grid. We evaluate repeated casting, compatibility with multichannel pipetting and automated imaging, directional tracer movement, and primary cortical neuron culture with retrograde axonal labeling. We further demonstrate that the parametric workflow generates coordinated fabrication files for alternative compartment geometries, providing a customizable strategy for manufacturing plate-format microfluidic devices.
Materials and Methods

Parametric design and fabrication-file generation - OpenMFD (https://github.com/trissim/OpenMFD) generated photomasks, insert arrays, wafer outlines, cutting guides, and plate frames from shared well, chamber, channel, and array dimensions (Figure 1). Device shapes were defined in OpenSCAD design software using the SolidPython library and exported as two-dimensional DXF mask drawings for each layer and three-dimensional STL models of the inserts and frames. Matching solid and hollow marks were used to align the photolithographic layers. The pin positions in the insert STL and the hole positions in the SUEX photomask came from the same coordinates, allowing the printed array to be aligned with the patterned wafer as a unit.

The tested design contained a 6 × 8 array of two-well units spaced 18 × 9 mm apart, giving 48 devices and 96 wells on a 9 mm grid. Each device had 62 microchannels with a design width of 10 µm and an interchannel gap of 30 µm. Matching masks and inserts received a horizontal scale factor of 1.0226 (2.26% enlargement) for the 100°C PDMS cure. Supplementary Table S3 gives the nominal device, channel, pin, taper, and frame dimensions used to generate the fabrication files.

OpenMFD also generated matched photomasks, inserts, wafer outlines, and frames for three literature-inspired layouts: oligodendrocyte myelination (PMID: 26015546), axon guidance with gradients at right angles to each other (PMID: 26000554), and a three-compartment assay (PMID: 24662423). These devices were not fabricated or biologically tested (Supplementary Table S3).

Fabrication of hybrid SU-8/SUEX and 3D-printed wafer molds - The mold comprised two 5 µm layers of SU-8 2005 liquid photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials), a 200 µm layer of SUEX K200 dry-film photoresist (DJ MicroLaminates), and a printed resin-insert array on a 6-inch silicon wafer (UniversityWafer ID857). These photoresists are light-sensitive resins used to pattern the mold features. SU-8 was spread by spinning the wafer (spin-coating) using a Laurell WS-650-8B, SUEX was laminated using an SK 335R6, and photolithographic layers were aligned and exposed using an EVG620. Unless otherwise noted, materials were processed according to the manufacturers’ instructions; the SU-8 2005 procedure targeted a 5 µm layer. Changes to the manufacturers’ procedures are described below and in Supplementary Protocol S2. No dehydration bake or HMDS adhesion-promoter treatment was used. Facility-supplied propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA) was the developer solvent used to remove unexposed material from both photoresists.
Layer 1 (base): SU-8 2005 was spin-coated to a 5 µm target thickness, flood-exposed without a mask, and left undeveloped beneath the patterned microchannel layer (Supplementary Note S2).

Layer 2 (microchannels): A second 5 µm SU-8 2005 layer was exposed through the microchannel photomask and developed. Before SUEX lamination, the wafer bearing the approximately 10 µm SU-8 stack was placed directly in an oven at 150°C for 10 min, then removed without controlled heating or cooling.

Layer 3 (wells): SUEX K200 dry film (200 µm) defined the well features and insert-alignment holes. The SUEX was exposed at 2800 mJ/cm² through an LP360 long-pass optical filter to block shorter-wavelength ultraviolet light. After exposure, the oven was heated from room temperature to 50°C at 1°C/min, held at 50°C for at least 12 h overnight, then switched off and allowed to cool. The wafer was submerged in developer and mixed for 20 min; the developer was replaced at 15 min. For the hard bake, the oven was heated to 120°C at 3°C/min, held for 30 min, then switched off and allowed to cool.

Well inserts were printed at their final relative positions using an Elegoo Mars 3 Pro and Siraya Tech Sculpt Clear resin. The profile used 20 µm layers, 5.5 s normal exposure, 50 s bottom exposure, 7 bottom layers, edge smoothing (anti-aliasing) at grey level 2, and no shrinkage or tolerance compensation in the print-preparation software. Supplementary Table S4 provides the remaining motion, timing, washing, and UV post-cure settings. Each insert had a 1.85 × 1.85 mm alignment pin corresponding to a 2.0 × 2.0 mm SUEX hole, giving 150 µm total clearance (75 µm per side).

The inserts were kept on a detachable flexible metal build plate so the whole array could be transferred at once. EPO-TEK 301-2 epoxy adhesive was applied around each pin, and the mold was positioned until the pins seated in their SUEX holes. An EPDM rubber sheet (0.03125 inch thick; Shore A hardness 60) between the fixed magnet and removable build plate provided a compressible backing; a second flat plate and clamps distributed pressure across the assembly (Figure 2). The clamped assembly was washed in two successive 1 min acetone baths, thoroughly blow-dried, and cured at room temperature for 48 h. After curing, the assembly was cleaned in an ultrasonic acetone bath for 10 min to remove residual material. The flexible metal build plate was flexed to release the bonded array (Supplementary Protocol S2).

After bonding, the hybrid mold received a 1 µm coating of the polymer parylene C to separate the printed resin and adhesive from the cast PDMS and aid release during demolding (PMID: 37534979; DOI: 10.1016/j.sna.2012.09.024). Parylene was deposited using a Specialty Coating Systems SCS 200 coater at the McGill Nanotools Microfab facility. The specified channel dimensions are the design dimensions before parylene coating.

PDMS casting and plate assembly - Frames were generated with the other fabrication files and printed in high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), a rubber-modified plastic, on an enclosed Creality K1C using a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.20 mm layers, a 220°C nozzle, and a 100°C build plate. The remaining printing settings are listed in Supplementary Table S6 and included in the supplied Creality Print 6.0.4 G-code printer-instruction file.

PDMS (Sylgard 184) was mixed at a 10:1 base:curing-agent ratio and poured over the full wafer within an aluminum-foil reservoir. The fill level remained below the insert tops to leave the wells open. Filled molds were supported in a six-shelf metal wafer rack, degassed until visible bubbles were removed (typically 10–30 min; approximately −15 inHg in our setup), and cured for 1 h at 100°C. Multiple molds could be degassed and cured in parallel.

The large mold features had tapered sidewalls to aid demolding, following the same design principle used in earlier multiscale PDMS molds (PMID: 20049640; DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ab16a7). The wafer was supported on a flat surface, and peeling proceeded from the corners toward the center while the PDMS was pulled backward to reduce local stress on the wafer.

A rectangular guide molded around the array was aligned to an industrial paper guillotine to trim each cast to 108 × 72 mm. The trimmed PDMS and a 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm coverslip-glass sheet were activated with dry-air plasma for 1 min at 200–600 mTorr in a Harrick PDC-001, brought into contact, and heated at 100°C for at least 1 min under uniform pressure (Supplementary Protocol S1).

The bonded PDMS-on-glass assembly was autoclaved in a sterilization pouch at 121°C for 15 min before frame assembly. The frame was decontaminated with 70% ethanol and inverted so that its adhesive groove faced upward. Henkel LOCTITE SI 5140 (3 oz tube, IDH 135264), a one-part silicone sealant that cures at room temperature, was dispensed into the groove (typically 0.5–1 mL per frame) (manufacturer technical data sheet). The bonded device was inverted with the glass facing upward and seated into the frame. After a 3-day room-temperature cure, the assembly was turned upright and excess adhesive was trimmed with a razor blade.

After adhesive curing, the assembled device received a second dry-air plasma treatment (Harrick PDC-001; high power, 30 W, 10 min, 400 mTorr) before aqueous coating and culture. This surface-treatment step was distinct from the earlier 1-min PDMS-glass bonding treatment.

Mold and device characterization - Each pin height was measured individually with a micrometer at all 96 positions of one 8 × 12 printed array before bonding. Supplementary Table S1 reports the individual values, mean, standard deviation, and difference between the tallest and shortest pins. Molds and casts were inspected to check that the SU-8/SUEX features remained attached, the inserts were seated and bonded, and the cast wells and microchannels were open and intact. Microscopy was used to inspect the channels after coating and casting. Supplementary Table S5 reports mold numbers and usable-cast yield separately and defines a usable cast.

Printed frames and assembled joints were inspected visually while selecting frame materials. Frame adhesives were screened by whether primary cortical-neuron cultures survived to the end of the experiment. Cell toxicity was not quantified.

To test whether cells could grow at the outer positions without the frame, one PDMS device was bonded to glass without a frame or frame adhesive and placed in a 14.5 cm-diameter polystyrene culture dish. This control removed both the frame assembly and the sealing effect of the frame adhesive.

Eight tips were fitted to a 12-channel pipette and aligned with one plate column to fill eight wells in parallel. Compatibility with plate-format imaging was tested by focusing and collecting images on Opera Phenix Plus and ImageXpress Micro Confocal microscopes at the Early Drug Discovery Unit (EDDU), The Neuro, McGill University, without custom plate handling or instrument modification.

Assessment of directional fluorescent tracer transport - Tracer distributions were compared immediately after loading and after 72 h in 24 two-compartment devices. Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated secondary antibody diluted 1:1000 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was loaded at 25 µL into the left compartment, and Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody diluted 1:1000 in PBS was loaded at 50 µL into the right compartment. The volume difference was established once, and the devices were kept in a cell-culture incubator for 72 h without replenishment or volume adjustment. Images were acquired in widefield mode using a 10× objective with a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.30, 2 × 2 camera binning, a 100 ms exposure, and red and green channels suited to the two fluorophores. Tracer movement was assessed visually by comparing green fluorescence appearing in the initially lower-volume compartment with red fluorescence appearing in the opposite compartment. Flow rate and the duration of the pressure difference were not measured.

Primary cortical neuron culture and retrograde axonal tracing - Primary cortical neurons were isolated from one embryonic day 18 (E18) Sprague Dawley rat embryo following Harris et al. (2007), then distributed across three separately assembled plates. Routine culture maintenance followed the cited protocol, with the device-specific conditions described below. The three plates were technical replicates of a single neuronal preparation. Dendritic polyglycerol amine (dPGA; DendroTEK Biosciences) was selected as the cell-attachment coating based on Clément et al. (2022). Wells were coated with 30 µL of 10 µg/mL dPGA for 10 min and washed once with water. Neurons were seeded into the cell-body (soma) compartment in 50 µL Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 5,000–10,000 cells per well, allowed to attach for at least 30 min, and then switched to supplemented Neurobasal Plus medium (1% N2, 2% B27, 1% glutamine). Volumes of 50 µL in the soma compartment and 25 µL in the axon compartment created a small pressure difference that directed fluid from the soma compartment toward the axon compartment during culture.

Cultures were maintained for 11 days in vitro (DIV11). At DIV10, Alexa Fluor-conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTβ-647) was applied to the lower-volume axon compartment at 1 µg/mL. CTβ-positive neuronal cell bodies were counted 24 h later, with one count per analyzed device. Analysis was restricted to the 24 interior devices on each plate because culture performance was poorer at the plate edges. Devices were excluded only when contamination or a technical failure prevented cell counting in the final image; high or low cell counts alone were not grounds for exclusion. Supplementary Protocol S1 provides the complete procedure.

High-content imaging and cell counting - CTβ images were collected at DIV11 in widefield mode on a PerkinElmer Opera Phenix Plus at EDDU using a 10×/0.30 NA objective, 2 × 2 camera binning, and laser autofocus. The effective pixel size was 1.187 µm. Brightfield images used a 10 ms exposure; Alexa 647 images used 640 nm excitation, 706 nm emission, and a 100 ms exposure.

For each device, images were collected at 35 positions (7 × 5 grid) on Plates 1 and 2 and 42 positions (7 × 6 grid) on Plate 3, with approximately 10% overlap. These images were stitched into one image per device. The PDMS array on Plate 3 was shifted slightly rightward during gluing, so a larger area was imaged to capture more microchannel exits. Each stitched image was aligned to a reference brightfield image and cropped to the same area for cell counting, regardless of the number of imaging positions. One cell count was recorded per analyzed device. These were baseline images collected before axotomy; Supplementary Protocol S1 describes the dataset. The supplementary files include the microscope’s saved settings and image positions for Plate 1 in XML format.

Statistical analysis - Supplementary Table S5 lists the numbers of molds and usable casts. All three culture plates contained neurons isolated from the same E18 rat embryo. The plates and the devices within them are therefore technical replicates. Figure 4C shows the mean number of CTβ-positive cell bodies per device for each plate, with the standard deviation across the analyzed interior devices. These summaries describe variation within this experiment.
Results

Parametric design enables coordinated fabrication of medium-throughput microfluidic arrays - We developed OpenMFD, a parametric design framework that integrates the generation of photolithographic masks, three-dimensional resin inserts, and supporting plate components within a common coordinate system (Fig. 1). The framework enables microchannel geometries, culture compartment dimensions, well positions, and device arrangements to be modified while maintaining the spatial relationships required for mold fabrication. In particular, the positions of the alignment pins on the printed resin inserts are matched to corresponding openings patterned in the SUEX layer, allowing complete insert arrays to be aligned with the photolithographically patterned silicon wafer.

To demonstrate this approach, we designed a medium-throughput platform comprising 48 independent, two-compartment microfluidic devices arranged in a 6 × 8 array (Fig. 1). Each device contained two culture wells connected by 62 parallel microchannels with nominal widths of 10 µm and interchannel gaps of 30 µm. The resulting array contained 96 wells positioned on a standard 9 mm microplate grid, providing a format compatible with multichannel liquid handling and automated plate-based microscopy. The coordinated design framework also incorporated a common dimensional scaling correction to account for PDMS shrinkage during curing.

To examine the adaptability of OpenMFD, we generated matching photomasks and resin-insert arrays for three additional microfluidic configurations: an oligodendrocyte myelination platform, an orthogonal-gradient axon-guidance platform, and a three-compartment neuronal culture platform (Fig. 5). Modifications to compartment number, well arrangement, and microchannel geometry were incorporated into the corresponding fabrication files while maintaining the alignment relationships between photolithographic and printed components. These examples establish the capacity of the design framework to generate coordinated fabrication files for distinct experimental configurations, although the additional designs were not physically fabricated or biologically evaluated.

Development and optimization of reusable hybrid wafer molds - The hybrid mold fabrication strategy combined photolithographically defined SU-8 microchannels and SUEX compartment structures with 3D-printed resin inserts that form the culture wells during PDMS casting (Fig. 2). A central requirement was the integration of micrometer-scale features with millimeter-scale structures while maintaining the integrity of the patterned wafer and enabling simultaneous positioning of the well-forming inserts.

Several fabrication challenges were identified and addressed during process development. Initial SUEX processing without an LP360 long-pass optical filter produced raised edges around patterned structures that interfered with contact between the resin inserts and their bonding surfaces. Incorporation of the long-pass filter reduced these surface irregularities and improved the apparent flatness of the SUEX structures, providing more suitable surfaces for insert attachment (Supplementary Note S1).

Adhesion of the photolithographically patterned microchannels presented a second challenge. SU-8 microchannel structures patterned directly onto bare silicon detached during subsequent processing. Introducing an underlying, uniformly exposed SU-8 layer prevented this observed detachment. Additional optimization was required to maintain layer integrity during SUEX lamination and thermal processing. In an initial development batch of eight wafers fabricated without a high-temperature SU-8 bake, some wafers exhibited warping and separation of patterned layers during cooling after SUEX processing. In contrast, both wafers fabricated in a subsequent batch incorporating a 150 °C bake for 10 min remained intact (Supplementary Note S2).

Simultaneous bonding of the resin inserts required accommodation of dimensional variation across the printed array. Measurements of 96 printed alignment pins revealed a mean height of 5.551 mm, a standard deviation of 26.7 µm, and a maximum height difference of 116 µm (Supplementary Table S1). Rigid clamping did not provide uniform contact across the insert array. Incorporating a compressible EPDM backing distributed the applied pressure and accommodated differences in insert height, enabling the pins to engage their corresponding SUEX alignment openings during a single bonding operation (Fig. 2).

The optimized process produced hybrid molds in which the photolithographic structures remained attached to the silicon substrate and the printed inserts were bonded in their designated positions. Following parylene C coating, cured PDMS could be released from the molds without additional silane-based release treatment. Microscopic inspection of the resulting PDMS casts confirmed the presence of open microchannels. However, the dimensional accuracy of the cast microchannels relative to their nominal photolithographic dimensions has not yet been quantitatively established.

Together, these optimizations enabled the integration of 96 well-forming resin inserts with wafer-scale photolithographically patterned microstructures, creating reusable hybrid molds suitable for repeated PDMS casting.

Repeated casting and assembly of plate-format microfluidic devices - The completed hybrid molds enabled the fabrication of PDMS devices containing all 48 compartmentalized culture units and 96 wells in a single casting operation (Fig. 3). Because the well-forming inserts remained attached to the mold, culture wells were generated directly during PDMS curing, eliminating the need for individual reservoir punching in subsequent production cycles. Multiple molds could be filled, degassed, and cured simultaneously, allowing parallel production of complete device arrays.

Five wafer-scale hybrid molds were assembled using the optimized fabrication procedure. Three molds entered routine use and collectively produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts (Supplementary Table S5). Of the remaining molds, one wafer fractured during demolding, while another was lost following PDMS leakage beneath the wafer and subsequent curing within the casting rack. The most recently fabricated molds remained in active use for more than eight months without visible deterioration of their structures.

PDMS casts were trimmed, plasma-bonded to glass, and incorporated into 3D-printed supporting frames to generate complete plate-format devices (Fig. 3). During development, both high-impact polystyrene (HIPS) and polypropylene were evaluated as frame materials. HIPS exhibited less visible warping under the printing conditions tested and was selected for subsequent device assembly.

The adhesive used to attach the glass-backed PDMS devices to the supporting frames was also found to influence biological compatibility. Among the adhesives evaluated, LOCTITE SI 5140 was the only formulation that supported primary cortical neuronal cultures through the experimental endpoint. The resulting adhesive joint remained visibly intact and leak-tight during routine handling and repeated incubator transfers. These observations were qualitative, and systematic measurements of adhesive cytotoxicity or joint mechanical strength were not performed.

Compatibility with multichannel liquid handling and automated imaging - The arrangement of the 96 culture wells on a standard 9 mm microplate grid enabled liquid handling using conventional multichannel pipettes (Fig. 1). Eight wells within a plate column could be filled simultaneously using a multichannel pipette, providing an alternative to the individual loading procedures commonly required for conventional compartmentalized microfluidic devices.

The assembled plates were compatible with two automated high-content imaging platforms, the Opera Phenix Plus and ImageXpress Micro Confocal. Both instruments successfully focused on and acquired images of the microfluidic arrays without modification to their plate-handling or imaging hardware. The Opera Phenix Plus was subsequently used for fluorescent tracer imaging and quantitative neuronal assays.

These observations demonstrate compatibility of the fabricated devices with standard multichannel liquid handling and automated image acquisition, providing the basis for parallelized experimental measurements across multiple compartmentalized cultures.

Directional fluid transport in compartmentalized devices - To assess fluid movement between the two culture compartments, we examined the redistribution of fluorescent tracers following the establishment of an initial volume difference between wells (Fig. 4A). Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated antibody was introduced into the lower-volume compartment (25 µL), while Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated antibody was introduced into the opposite compartment (50 µL). Tracer distributions were examined in 24 devices immediately after loading and following 72 h of incubation without further volume adjustment.

At the initial imaging time point, the two fluorophores were predominantly localized to their respective loading compartments. After 72 h, green fluorescence was observed in the initially lower-volume compartment, whereas comparatively little red fluorescence was visible in the opposite compartment (Fig. 4A). This redistribution was consistent with net tracer movement in the direction established by the initial hydrostatic volume difference.

These observations demonstrate that the connecting microchannels permit tracer transport between compartments and that an initial difference in fluid volume can produce directional redistribution. However, the experimental design did not determine the magnitude or duration of fluid flow, and compartmental isolation throughout the 72 h interval was not established.

Validation of primary neuronal culture and retrograde axonal labeling - We next evaluated the suitability of the fabricated microfluidic devices for compartmentalized primary neuronal culture. Embryonic rat cortical neurons were seeded into the somatic compartments of three independently assembled plates and maintained for 11 days in vitro (DIV11). The three plates contained neurons derived from a single embryonic preparation and therefore represented technical replicates.

At DIV10, fluorescently conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTβ-647) was applied selectively to the axonal compartments. Following 24 h of incubation, fluorescently labeled neuronal cell bodies were detected within the somatic compartments (Fig. 4B). The appearance of CTβ-positive cell bodies following tracer application to the axonal compartment was consistent with uptake by axons extending through the microchannels and subsequent retrograde transport to neuronal somata.

Neuronal culture performance varied with position within the assembled plates, with poorer growth observed in peripheral devices. Quantitative analysis was therefore restricted to the 24 interior devices on each plate. Of the 72 interior devices across the three plates, three were excluded because contamination or technical failures prevented reliable cell counting, leaving 69 devices for analysis.

CTβ-positive neuronal cell bodies were quantified from standardized image regions acquired by automated high-content microscopy. The mean number of labeled cell bodies per device and the corresponding within-plate standard deviations are presented for each of the three plates in Fig. 4C. These measurements demonstrate the feasibility of collecting quantitative retrograde labeling data across multiple compartmentalized neuronal cultures using an automated imaging workflow.

To investigate the reduced neuronal growth at peripheral positions, an additional PDMS device was bonded directly to glass and maintained in a conventional culture dish without the supporting frame or frame adhesive. In this configuration, neuronal growth at peripheral positions appeared comparable to that in more central regions. Although this observation suggests that peripheral devices can support neuronal culture, the relative contributions of frame geometry, adhesive exposure, sealing, and culture environment to the reduced growth observed in assembled plates remain unresolved.

Collectively, these experiments establish the compatibility of the microfluidic platform with primary cortical neuronal culture, compartment-specific axonal labeling, and automated quantitative imaging. Further experiments using independent neuronal preparations will be required to determine biological reproducibility across cultures.
Discussion

The hybrid fabrication strategy developed in this study provides a scalable approach for producing compartmentalized microfluidic culture devices by integrating photolithographically defined microfeatures with 3D-printed, millimeter-scale structures on reusable silicon-wafer molds. Building on previous advances in multiscale molding and the elimination of manual reservoir punching, our approach introduces a coordinated parametric design framework that enables the simultaneous alignment and attachment of large arrays of well-forming inserts to patterned wafers. This strategy addresses a practical limitation of conventional PDMS microfluidic fabrication, in which high-resolution microchannels can be reproduced by soft lithography, but the formation of individual culture wells frequently requires additional processing after casting. By incorporating all well-forming structures into a reusable mold, the method separates the specialized fabrication steps required to construct the mold from subsequent production of complete microfluidic devices. The resulting platform combines customizable microfluidic geometries with a standardized plate format suitable for medium-throughput biological experimentation.

Previous approaches have demonstrated the feasibility of combining micrometer- and millimeter-scale features using hybrid soft lithography, alternative molding strategies, and additive manufacturing (PMIDs: 20049640; 32832365). Particularly relevant to our approach, Ristola and colleagues incorporated individually aligned 3D-printed metal inserts into SU-8 molds to fabricate compartmentalized neuron–oligodendrocyte culture devices (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ab16a7). Our method extends this principle through a common parametric design framework that generates matching photomasks, alignment features, and resin-insert arrays, permitting all 96 inserts to be positioned in a single alignment operation. The use of corresponding square alignment pins and SUEX openings constrains lateral displacement during assembly, while a compressible backing accommodates variations in insert height. In the present design, the nominal lateral clearance was 75 µm per side, substantially smaller than the 1.275 mm margin between the microchannel array and surrounding chamber boundaries. Although these geometrical relationships provide tolerance for insert positioning, the actual alignment accuracy remains dependent on photolithographic registration and resin-printing precision and was not directly quantified. Importantly, the same array-transfer procedure can be applied to different numbers and arrangements of inserts, provided the complete array remains compatible with the wafer and printer dimensions.

The combination of photolithography and resin printing also exploits the complementary capabilities of these fabrication technologies. Photolithography remains well suited to defining micrometer-scale structures, whereas resin printing provides an accessible means of producing larger three-dimensional features. Recent developments in printed molds and hybrid fabrication have expanded the range of structures that can be manufactured for biological microfluidic applications, although achievable resolution, PDMS curing compatibility, and surface treatment remain important considerations (PMIDs: 40190179; 40667579). In our approach, the printed resin inserts remain permanently attached to the silicon-wafer mold rather than becoming components of the finished culture device. A conformal parylene C coating separates the printed resin and adhesive from the cast PDMS and facilitates repeated demolding. The suitability of parylene C as a protective coating for resin-printed components has also been demonstrated in biological applications (PMID: 37534979). Consequently, the finished culture surfaces comprise PDMS bonded to glass, while the printed components are confined to the reusable manufacturing tool. This distinction is potentially advantageous for applications requiring conventional PDMS surface treatments and established neuronal culture protocols, although the biological compatibility of each assembled device configuration must still be established experimentally.

The fabrication results demonstrate the feasibility of repeated production using the hybrid molds. Three molds collectively produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts, and the most recently fabricated molds remained in active use for more than eight months without visible deterioration. Several processing modifications were important for achieving this performance, including the use of a continuous SU-8 base layer, optimized thermal processing, filtered SUEX exposure, compressible clamping, and a flexible build plate for releasing the bonded insert array. These modifications addressed distinct challenges involving photoresist adhesion, bonding-surface uniformity, printed insert-height variation, and mechanical stress during assembly. Once a mold was completed, subsequent production required only PDMS casting, demolding, glass bonding, and plate assembly, without repeating photolithography or individually punching culture wells. This separation of mold fabrication from repeated device production may improve accessibility for laboratories that can obtain molds through a shared microfabrication facility but do not have routine access to cleanroom equipment. Nevertheless, the present study did not directly quantify manufacturing time, labor requirements, or cost savings relative to established alternatives, and these potential advantages should be evaluated in future comparisons.

The compatibility of the resulting devices with conventional laboratory workflows is an important practical outcome. The 48-device array provides 96 culture wells on a standard 9 mm microplate grid, enabling multichannel pipetting and automated high-content imaging without instrument modification. Previous studies have demonstrated the value of parallelized and modular microfluidic systems for neuronal experimentation (PMIDs: 38150531; 35466333; 38841815). Our approach complements these platforms by providing an alternative fabrication strategy rather than introducing neuronal compartmentalization or medium-throughput culture as new capabilities. The demonstration of directional fluorescent tracer redistribution and retrograde CTβ labeling confirms that the fabricated devices support fluid movement through the connecting microchannels and compartment-specific neuronal manipulations. However, the tracer experiment did not establish the duration of hydrostatic flow or quantitatively measure fluidic isolation. Similarly, neuronal experiments using 69 interior devices across three plates demonstrate assay feasibility but were performed using a single embryonic neuronal preparation. Validation across independent preparations and additional functional assays will be necessary to establish biological reproducibility and suitability for screening applications.

Several design considerations remain important when adapting the platform to other experimental configurations. The current mold incorporates a 2.26% dimensional scaling correction to compensate for PDMS shrinkage, but the dimensions of the finished microchannels have not been quantitatively characterized. In addition, the 1 µm parylene coating is expected to increase the width of a channel-forming ridge by approximately 2 µm, assuming uniform deposition, while leaving its height relative to the surrounding coated surface approximately unchanged. These geometrical effects may be significant for microchannels with nominal widths of 10 µm. Direct measurements of coated mold features and the resulting PDMS channels would establish dimensional fidelity and permit refinement of the scaling parameters. The geometry of the well-forming inserts also introduces practical constraints. Tapered sidewalls facilitate demolding but reduce the available reservoir dimensions at fixed well spacing, limiting the present design to a maximum working volume of approximately 50 µL per well. Increasing reservoir capacity would require balancing well dimensions, wall thickness, demolding performance, and the dimensions and cost of the supporting glass substrate.

The supporting plate frame represents another opportunity for optimization. Although assembled devices supported routine handling, automated imaging, and neuronal culture, neuronal growth was reduced at peripheral positions. In an unframed PDMS-on-glass device maintained in a conventional culture dish, peripheral cultures appeared comparable to those at interior positions, suggesting that this limitation is not necessarily intrinsic to the compartmentalized PDMS geometry. However, this observation does not distinguish the potential contributions of frame geometry, adhesive exposure, sealing, or the surrounding culture environment. Modifying the frame and its assembly procedure independently of the reusable mold should allow these factors to be investigated without redesigning the microfluidic structures. Resolving this limitation will be important for achieving reliable biological performance across the complete 48-device array.

Finally, the open-source parametric framework provides a means of extending the fabrication strategy beyond the two-compartment neuronal platform demonstrated here. OpenMFD generated coordinated fabrication files for oligodendrocyte myelination, axon-guidance, and three-compartment neuronal culture configurations, illustrating how compartment geometry and microchannel organization can be modified while preserving alignment between photolithographic and printed mold components. These designs have not yet been fabricated, and changes in insert geometry, well spacing, or compartment arrangement will require validation of alignment, casting, demolding, fluid transport, and biological compatibility. Nevertheless, the ability to generate coordinated fabrication components from shared design parameters reduces the need to redesign individual mold elements independently. By combining high-resolution photolithography, array-scale integration of 3D-printed inserts, and repeated PDMS casting, this approach provides a flexible foundation for developing customized medium-throughput microfluidic devices while retaining compatibility with established laboratory workflows.
Conclusions

We developed an open-source hybrid fabrication strategy that combines high-resolution photolithography with 3D-printed resin inserts to produce reusable silicon-wafer molds for medium-throughput microfluidic devices. By integrating parametric design with simultaneous alignment of well-forming inserts, this approach enables repeated fabrication of compartmentalized PDMS devices without individual reservoir punching. The resulting platform accommodates 48 independent microfluidic devices with 96 wells arranged in a standard microplate format, supporting multichannel liquid handling, automated high-content imaging, and compartmentalized neuronal culture. Repeated casting demonstrated mold durability, while retrograde axonal labeling established compatibility with neuronal assays. Although further optimization is required to improve peripheral culture performance and establish quantitative fabrication reproducibility, this approach provides an adaptable and accessible framework for producing customized microfluidic platforms for neuroscience and other applications requiring spatially controlled cell culture.
